headline: A startup called Nolla Health has begun using AI to scan faces and write acne prescriptions in Utah, with less doctor checking as the pilot grows.
score_reason: Pool 8 kept: a reported US first for AI writing first-time prescriptions, though a one-state pilot with company-supplied claims.
importance_line: People in Utah with mild-to-moderate acne can now get a prescription from an app instead of a doctor's visit, making this an early test of whether AI can safely start a treatment rather than just renew one, though it is a small pilot, doctor checks ease as it grows, and no results or independent safety data are reported.
summary: The Verge reports, citing Nolla Health's announcement and an earlier Bloomberg report, that adults in Utah with mild-to-moderate acne can now pay $4.99 a month for an app in which AI scans their face, judges the acne and writes the prescription, and that the company says it is the first in the US to have AI issue first-time prescriptions rather than renewals. Nolla Health says oversight will ease: two doctors approve each of the first 100 prescriptions before they are issued, then review them after the fact, and past 500 patients check a monthly sample of at least 10% plus any case with a side effect or escalation.
notes: Full text read from fulltext/C10-01.txt. Credit chain not fully clear (Nolla Health press release, Bloomberg earlier, The Verge), so both outlets are named. Utah's sign-off is The Verge's statement; no state source read.
